content: Rotavirus is a virus that primarily causes severe diarrhea in infants and young children. This condition is often accompanied by vomiting and fever. While rotavirus is not the only cause of severe diarrhea, it is one of the most serious. Most children are infected with rotavirus before their fifth birthday. The disease is more common during the months of November through May, depending on the region. Children can contract rotavirus by being in close contact with other infected children. Improved hygiene and sanitation practices have not been very effective in reducing the incidence of rotavirus disease. The rotavirus vaccine is the most effective way to protect children against this illness. This vaccine is administered orally, meaning it is swallowed rather than injected. While the vaccine does not prevent diarrhea or vomiting caused by other pathogens, it is highly effective at preventing these symptoms when caused by rotavirus. Approximately 98% of children who receive the vaccine are protected from severe rotavirus diarrhea, and about 74% do not develop rotavirus diarrhea at all. Vaccinated children are also significantly less likely to require hospitalization or medical visits due to rotavirus infection. Children should receive three doses of the rotavirus vaccine. These doses are recommended at the ages of 2 months, 4 months, and 6 months. The first dose should be administered between 6 and 12 weeks of age, as the vaccine has not been studied for use in children outside this age range. All three doses should be completed by 32 weeks of age. The rotavirus vaccine can be given at the same time as other routine childhood vaccines, and children can be fed normally after receiving the vaccine. Certain children should not receive the rotavirus vaccine or should delay vaccination. A child who has experienced a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction to a previous dose of the rotavirus vaccine or to any of its components should not receive additional doses. Parents should inform their doctor of any known severe allergies in their child. Children who are moderately or severely ill at the time of vaccination, including those with diarrhea or vomiting, should wait until they recover before receiving the vaccine. However, children with mild illnesses can usually be vaccinated. Parents should consult their doctor if their child has ongoing digestive problems, a weakened immune system due to conditions such as HIV/AIDS or cancer, or if the child is undergoing treatments like long-term steroid use or chemotherapy. Additionally, parents should inform their doctor if their child has recently received a blood transfusion or other blood products, such as immune globulin. In the late 1990s, a different type of rotavirus vaccine was associated with an uncommon form of bowel obstruction called intussusception and was subsequently withdrawn from the market. The current rotavirus vaccine has been tested in over 70,000 children and has not been linked to intussusception. However, children who have previously experienced intussusception from any cause are at a higher risk of recurrence and, as a precaution, should not receive the rotavirus vaccine. Like any medication, vaccines can potentially cause serious side effects, such as severe allergic reactions. However, the risk of the rotavirus vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely low. Receiving the vaccine is much safer than contracting the disease itself. Mild side effects, such as temporary diarrhea or vomiting, occur slightly more often (1-3%) in vaccinated children within seven days of receiving a dose compared to unvaccinated children. Moderate or severe problems have not been associated with this vaccine. Rare reactions, if they occur, may not be identified until the vaccine has been used by thousands or millions of people. As with all vaccines, the rotavirus vaccine will continue to be monitored for any unusual or severe problems. Parents should watch for any unusual conditions following vaccination, such as high fever or changes in behavior. Signs of a severe allergic reaction may include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, a rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. If any of these symptoms occur, parents should seek medical attention immediately and inform the doctor of the date and time of the reaction and when the vaccine was administered. They should also ask their healthcare provider to file a Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) form or contact VAERS directly at 1-800-822-7967 or through their website. In the rare event of a serious reaction to a vaccine, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) is available to help cover the costs of care for those affected. For more information about the VICP, parents can call 1-800-338-2382 or visit the program's website. For additional information about the rotavirus vaccine, parents are encouraged to consult their doctor or healthcare provider, who can provide the vaccine package insert or recommend other reliable sources. They can also contact their local or state health department’s immunization program or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) at 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visit the National Immunization Program’s website.
